Objective: State what training can and cannot responsibly do for this rollout right now — name the one performance objective that is teachable today, flag the objective that matters most (disagreement handling) as currently unteachable, and give the first concrete session, its instructor, and the date it must be piloted by. This is not a full curriculum, because the inputs a curriculum needs do not exist yet.

Body: Before I say what I'll build, two things I'm assuming rather than citing as settled fact: that the resistance described is a Desire-stage problem in ADKAR terms rather than a Knowledge gap, and that the "who wins when technician and copilot disagree" question sits with whoever ends up owning process design. Neither has been confirmed by another workstream — no business owner is named, no readiness assessment exists. I'm building on inference, and if either assumption is wrong, this design needs to be revisited.

Given that, the objective that matters most — *given a flagged work order and the copilot's confidence score, the technician decides to act, defer, or escalate, and records why* — cannot be assessed today. There is no escalation handoff and no confirmed human-in-loop trust boundary in whatever target architecture eventually gets chosen. Until "escalate to whom, on what evidence, with what override authority" exists as a real process, I cannot teach to it or check whether anyone learned it. I will not present a completion certificate for this as capability.

What I can build now, safely, is a shorter orientation, not a curriculum: **"Copilot Trust Boundary & What Changes for You"** — one 90-minute session per cohort, capped at 12 technicians plus their line manager together, because the manager's stance in the room matters as much as the content.

- **Inductive (20 min):** Technicians walk through how they diagnose a hard fault today — manuals, tribal knowledge, a call to a senior tech. This expertise is being asked to sit next to a tool, not be replaced by it, and it needs naming before anything new is introduced.
- **Input (20 min):** What the copilot does and doesn't do — advisory only, what the confidence score means, and an explicit statement that the technician remains the decision-maker and the field service record of truth is unchanged until proven otherwise.
- **Implementation (35 min):** Technicians work through 4–5 real pilot cases, narrating act/defer/escalate decisions aloud. These cases come from pilot repair logs with known data quality issues — labeled illustrative, not validated, until a golden dataset exists.
- **Integration (15 min):** What happens back on the floor next week. This is the weakest phase right now — there is no escalation path to send them back into — and I will say that gap out loud in the room rather than paper over it.

Who teaches: a named senior technician from the pilot cohort, co-facilitating with L&D — not a vendor applications engineer delivering it once and disappearing. If the vendor is the only available instructor, that is a one-cohort design with no path for the next site, and I will not let it be presented as scalable.

Citations: ADKAR model, the basis for the Desire-vs-Knowledge assumption this design defers to — https://www.prosci.com/methodology/adkar ; Kolb's experiential learning cycle, the underlying theory our team's Inductive/Input/Implementation/Integration labels are built on (the specific 4-I naming is our internal convention, not a direct citation) — https://www.simplypsychology.org/learning-kolb.html

Risks: (1) The escalation process and trust boundary are unresolved, so the core objective is currently unassessable — running only the orientation and calling it "rollout training" would misrepresent readiness. (2) No instructor exists beyond a possible single vendor delivery; without a second facilitator identified, there is no second cohort. (3) No line manager has agreed to release the 90 minutes plus their own attendance; given reported resistance, treat this as unconfirmed until a manager commits in writing. (4) Case material comes from pilot logs with known data quality issues — technicians may practice on flawed examples and generalize wrongly. (5) If this session runs before headcount implications are disclosed, I will not run it — that conversation belongs to Change Management, not a training room, and skipping it will surface as anger in session rather than before it.

Next Steps: (1) I will start sourcing a named senior-technician co-facilitator now; realistically this depends on a line manager agreeing to release someone, which is not secured, so treat two weeks as a target, not a commitment, until that release is confirmed. (2) No date exists yet for the escalation handoff or trust-boundary sign-off — until a business owner and a process lead are named, I need whoever is appointed to give me a real delivery date before I schedule a pilot against it. (3) Pilot the orientation with one 12-person cohort, technicians and their manager together, only after that handoff and boundary are delivered — not before. (4) Report to the named business owner, once appointed, that full curriculum design is blocked on three inputs: escalation process, trust-boundary sign-off, and confirmed manager time release — and that an orientation completion count must never be reported as "technicians trained."
